Fourier Series

Purdue University
Course-material provenance

This page was migrated from the CHM 696 course materials developed by Jonathan Hood and Lyudmila Slipchenko. Equations and examples remain under editorial review during the Fall 2026 website migration.

Learning goals¶

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

  • compute real and complex Fourier-series coefficients;

  • use parity and orthogonality to simplify a series;

  • state what a Fourier series converges to at smooth points and jump discontinuities; and

  • explain how the continuous Fourier transform emerges as the period tends to infinity.

Introduction¶

  • Fourier series are a powerful mathematical tool used to represent periodic functions as infinite sums of trigonometric functions.

  • Under appropriate integrability conditions, a periodic function can be represented in a mean-square sense by sine and cosine modes. Pointwise convergence requires additional conditions and behaves specially at jumps.

  • This decomposition allows analysis of complex periodic phenomena using their simpler constituent parts.

The general form of a Fourier series for a function f(x)f(x)f(x) with period 2L2L2L is:

f(x)=a02+∑n=1∞(ancos⁡(nωx)+bnsin⁡(nωx))f(x) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (a_n \cos(n\omega x) + b_n \sin(n\omega x))f(x)=2a0​​+n=1∑∞​(an​cos(nωx)+bn​sin(nωx))
(1)

  • ω=2π2L=πL\omega = \frac{2\pi}{2L} = \frac{\pi}{L}ω=2L2π​=Lπ​ is the fundamental frequency.

  • LLL is half the period.

  • a02\frac{a_0}{2}2a0​​ represents the mean value of the function over one period.

  • cos⁡(nωx)\cos(n\omega x)cos(nωx) and sin⁡(nωx)\sin(n\omega x)sin(nωx) are harmonic components of the function, nnn is the harmonic number.

  • ana_nan​ and bnb_nbn​ determine the amplitude of each harmonic component.

Fourier series¶

The Fourier coefficients a0a_0a0​, ana_nan​, and bnb_nbn​ are determined as:

a0=1L∫−LLf(x)dxan=1L∫−LLf(x)cos⁡(nωx)dx(n=1,2,3,...)bn=1L∫−LLf(x)sin⁡(nωx)dx(n=1,2,3,...)\begin{aligned} a_0 &= \frac{1}{L} \int_{-L}^{L} f(x) dx \\ a_n &= \frac{1}{L} \int_{-L}^{L} f(x) \cos(n\omega x) dx \quad (n = 1, 2, 3, ...) \\ b_n &= \frac{1}{L} \int_{-L}^{L} f(x) \sin(n\omega x) dx \quad (n = 1, 2, 3, ...) \end{aligned}a0​an​bn​​=L1​∫−LL​f(x)dx=L1​∫−LL​f(x)cos(nωx)dx(n=1,2,3,...)=L1​∫−LL​f(x)sin(nωx)dx(n=1,2,3,...)​
(2)

  • These integrals effectively "project" the function onto the basis of sines and cosines, determining how much of each frequency component is present in the original function.

  • This projection is possible due to the orthogonality of the trigonometric functions.

  • The approximation of the original function generally improves as more terms are included in the Fourier series. The rate of convergence depends on the smoothness of the function being approximated.

Properties of Fourier Series: Orthogonality¶

A key property that makes Fourier series so useful is the orthogonality of the trigonometric functions. This property allows us to separate different frequency components of a function, simplifying analysis and computations. Over an interval of one period, we have:

∫−LLsin⁡(nωx)sin⁡(mωx) dx=Lδnm∫−LLcos⁡(nωx)cos⁡(mωx) dx=Lδnm∫−LLsin⁡(nωx)cos⁡(mωx) dx=0\begin{aligned} \int_{-L}^{L} \sin(n\omega x) \sin(m\omega x) \, dx &= L \delta_{nm} \\ \int_{-L}^{L} \cos(n\omega x) \cos(m\omega x) \, dx &= L \delta_{nm} \\ \int_{-L}^{L} \sin(n\omega x) \cos(m\omega x) \, dx &= 0 \end{aligned}∫−LL​sin(nωx)sin(mωx)dx∫−LL​cos(nωx)cos(mωx)dx∫−LL​sin(nωx)cos(mωx)dx​=Lδnm​=Lδnm​=0​
(3)

for positive integers m,nm,nm,n. The constant mode must be treated separately: ∫−LL1 dx=2L\int_{-L}^{L}1\,dx=2L∫−LL​1dx=2L. Here δnm\delta_{nm}δnm​ is the Kronecker delta,

δnm={1if n=m0if n≠m\delta_{nm} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } n = m \\ 0 & \text{if } n \neq m \end{cases}δnm​={10​if n=mif n=m​
(4)

This orthogonality is what allows us to separate the different frequency components of a function.

Properties of Fourier Series: Odd and Even Functions¶

The symmetry of a function can significantly simplify its Fourier series representation. This simplification occurs because odd functions only have sine components, while even functions only have cosine components:

  • For odd functions [f(−x)=−f(x)f(-x) = -f(x)f(−x)=−f(x)]:

    • Only sine terms are present (bn≠0b_n \neq 0bn​=0, an=0a_n = 0an​=0)

    • The series simplifies to: f(x)=∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nωx)f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n \sin(n\omega x)f(x)=∑n=1∞​bn​sin(nωx)

  • For even functions [f(−x)=f(x)f(-x) = f(x)f(−x)=f(x)]:

    • Only cosine terms are present (an≠0a_n \neq 0an​=0, bn=0b_n = 0bn​=0)

    • The series simplifies to: f(x)=a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nωx)f(x) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \cos(n\omega x)f(x)=2a0​​+∑n=1∞​an​cos(nωx)

These simplifications occur because the integrals for the Fourier coefficients of the opposite type (cosine for odd functions, sine for even functions) evaluate to zero due to the symmetry of the function.

The complex form of Fourier series¶

The complex form of the Fourier series is given by:

f(x)=∑n=−∞∞Cneinωxf(x) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} C_n e^{in\omega x}f(x)=n=−∞∑∞​Cn​einωx
(5)

The complex coefficients CnC_nCn​ are determined by:

Cn=12L∫−LLf(x)e−inωx dxC_n = \frac{1}{2L} \int_{-L}^L f(x) e^{-in\omega x} \, dxCn​=2L1​∫−LL​f(x)e−inωxdx
(6)

These coefficients relate to the real coefficients ana_nan​ and bnb_nbn​ as follows:

C0=a02(represents the mean value of f(x))Cn=an−ibn2for n>0C−n=an+ibn2for n>0\begin{aligned} C_0 &= \frac{a_0}{2} \quad \text{(represents the mean value of } f(x) \text{)} \\ C_n &= \frac{a_n - ib_n}{2} \quad \text{for } n > 0 \\ C_{-n} &= \frac{a_n + ib_n}{2} \quad \text{for } n > 0 \end{aligned}C0​Cn​C−n​​=2a0​​(represents the mean value of f(x))=2an​−ibn​​for n>0=2an​+ibn​​for n>0​
(7)

These relationships allow for conversion between the complex and real forms of the Fourier series.

Properties of Complex Fourier Series¶

  • For real functions f(x)f(x)f(x), we have C−n=Cn∗C_{-n} = C_n^*C−n​=Cn∗​ (complex conjugate). This property ensures that the function remains real when the complex exponentials are summed.

  • The complex exponentials are orthogonal:

12L∫−LLeimωxe−inωx dx=δmn.\frac{1}{2L} \int_{-L}^L e^{im\omega x} e^{-in\omega x} \, dx = \delta_{mn}.2L1​∫−LL​eimωxe−inωxdx=δmn​.
(8)

This orthogonality is analogous to that of sine and cosine functions in the real form.

Advantages of the Complex Form¶

The complex form of Fourier series offers several advantages:

  • More compact notation, combining sine and cosine terms into a single expression.

  • Often simplifies mathematical manipulations, especially in advanced applications.

  • Provides a natural bridge to the Fourier transform in more advanced studies.

  • Facilitates easier handling of symmetry properties in certain types of problems.

Example¶

Consider the square wave function:

f(x)={1,0<x<L−1,−L<x<0f(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & 0 < x < L \\ -1, & -L < x < 0 \end{cases}f(x)={1,−1,​0<x<L−L<x<0​
(9)
Note

The displayed formula defines one period on (−L,L)(-L,L)(−L,L). It is understood to be continued periodically with period 2L2L2L outside that interval.

Its complex Fourier series is:

f(x)=4π∑n=1,3,5,…∞1nsin⁡(nωx)=−2iπ∑n=−∞n odd∞einωxn.f(x) = \frac{4}{\pi} \sum_{n=1,3,5,\ldots}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n} \sin(n\omega x) = -\frac{2i}{\pi} \sum_{\substack{n=-\infty\\ n\ \mathrm{odd}}}^{\infty} \frac{e^{in\omega x}}{n}.f(x)=π4​n=1,3,5,…∑∞​n1​sin(nωx)=−π2i​n=−∞n odd​∑∞​neinωx​.
(10)

This example demonstrates how the complex form can provide a concise representation of a discontinuous function.

Convergence of Fourier Series: The Dirichlet Conditions¶

The Dirichlet conditions provide convenient sufficient (but not necessary) conditions for pointwise convergence of a Fourier series. For a periodic function satisfying these conditions, the series converges at xxx to [f(x−)+f(x+)]/2[f(x^-)+f(x^+)]/2[f(x−)+f(x+)]/2:

  1. f(x)f(x)f(x) is periodic with period 2L2L2L

  2. f(x)f(x)f(x) is single-valued and has a finite number of discontinuities in [−L,L][-L, L][−L,L]

  3. f(x)f(x)f(x) has a finite number of maxima and minima in [−L,L][-L, L][−L,L]

  4. ∫−LL∣f(x)∣ dx\int_{-L}^L |f(x)| \, dx∫−LL​∣f(x)∣dx is finite

At a point where fff is continuous, this limiting value is simply f(x)f(x)f(x).

Fourier Transform¶

The Fourier series for a function f(x)f(x)f(x) defined on the interval [−L,L][-L, L][−L,L] is:

f(x)=∑n=−∞∞cneinπLxf(x) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n e^{i \frac{n\pi}{L} x}f(x)=n=−∞∑∞​cn​eiLnπ​x
(11)

where the Fourier coefficients cnc_ncn​ are defined as:

cn=12L∫−LLf(x)e−inπLx dxc_n = \frac{1}{2L} \int_{-L}^{L} f(x) e^{-i \frac{n\pi}{L} x} \, dxcn​=2L1​∫−LL​f(x)e−iLnπ​xdx
(12)

Define the continuous wave number kkk as:

k=nπLk = \frac{n\pi}{L}k=Lnπ​
(13)

This implies that n=kLπn = \frac{kL}{\pi}n=πkL​. The spacing between adjacent kkk-values is:

Δk=πL\Delta k = \frac{\pi}{L}Δk=Lπ​
(14)

Fourier Transform (continued)¶

As L→∞L\to\inftyL→∞, the wave-number spacing tends to zero and

Δk=πL,∑nΔk⟶∫−∞∞dk.\Delta k=\frac{\pi}{L}, \qquad \sum_n \Delta k \longrightarrow \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dk.Δk=Lπ​,n∑​Δk⟶∫−∞∞​dk.
(15)

Choose the transform convention

F(k)=∫−∞∞f(x)e−ikx dx.F(k)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx.F(k)=∫−∞∞​f(x)e−ikxdx.
(16)

For finite LLL, the sampled transform and Fourier coefficient satisfy

F(kn)=2L cn,kn=nπL.F(k_n)=2L\,c_n, \qquad k_n=\frac{n\pi}{L}.F(kn​)=2Lcn​,kn​=Lnπ​.
(17)

Therefore

f(x)=∑nΔk2πF(kn)eiknx⟶12π∫−∞∞F(k)eikx dk.f(x) =\sum_n \frac{\Delta k}{2\pi}F(k_n)e^{ik_nx} \longrightarrow \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(k)e^{ikx}\,dk.f(x)=n∑​2πΔk​F(kn​)eikn​x⟶2π1​∫−∞∞​F(k)eikxdk.
(18)

Fourier Transform (continued)¶

The forward and inverse Fourier transforms are thus given by:

Forward Fourier Transform:

F(k)=∫−∞∞f(x)e−ikx dxF(k) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) e^{-i k x} \, dxF(k)=∫−∞∞​f(x)e−ikxdx
(19)

Inverse Fourier Transform:

f(x)=12π∫−∞∞F(k)eikx dkf(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(k)e^{ikx}\,dkf(x)=2π1​∫−∞∞​F(k)eikxdk
(20)

Other conventions move the factor of 2π2\pi2π to the forward transform or split it symmetrically as 1/2π1/\sqrt{2\pi}1/2π​ in both directions.

[Physically, the Fourier transform decomposes a function into its constituent frequencies, allowing us to analyze signals in the frequency domain rather than the time domain.]{style=“color: blue”}

Comparison of Fourier Series and Fourier Transform¶

Fourier Series Fourier Transform

f(x)=∑n=−∞∞cneinω0xf(x) = \sum\limits_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n e^{in\omega_0 x}f(x)=n=−∞∑∞​cn​einω0​x f(x)=12π∫−∞∞F(ω)eiωxdωf(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int\limits_{-\infty}^{\infty} F(\omega) e^{i\omega x} d\omegaf(x)=2π1​−∞∫∞​F(ω)eiωxdω cn=1T∫−T/2T/2f(x)e−inω0xdxc_n = \frac{1}{T} \int\limits_{-T/2}^{T/2} f(x) e^{-in\omega_0 x} dxcn​=T1​−T/2∫T/2​f(x)e−inω0​xdx F(ω)=∫−∞∞f(x)e−iωxdxF(\omega) = \int\limits_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) e^{-i\omega x} dxF(ω)=−∞∫∞​f(x)e−iωxdx

Example 1: Transform of eiω0te^i\omega_0teiω0​t¶

Example 1: Transform of eiω0te^{i\omega_0t}eiω0​t

f(t)=eiω0tF(ω)=∫−∞∞eiω0te−iωtdt=∫−∞∞ei(ω0−ω)tdt=2πδ(ω−ω0)\begin{aligned} f(t) &= e^{i\omega_0t} \\[1ex] F(\omega) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{i\omega_0t} e^{-i\omega t} dt = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{i(\omega_0-\omega)t} dt \\[1ex] &= 2\pi \delta(\omega-\omega_0) \end{aligned}f(t)F(ω)​=eiω0​t=∫−∞∞​eiω0​te−iωtdt=∫−∞∞​ei(ω0​−ω)tdt=2πδ(ω−ω0​)​
(21)

This identity is understood in the sense of distributions, not as an ordinary improper integral. It states that a pure complex exponential has all of its spectral weight at the single frequency ω0\omega_0ω0​.

Delta Function¶

The Dirac delta function δ(x)\delta(x)δ(x) is a generalized function that has the following properties:

  • δ(x)=0\delta(x) = 0δ(x)=0 for all x≠0x \neq 0x=0

  • ∫−∞∞δ(x)dx=1\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x) dx = 1∫−∞∞​δ(x)dx=1

  • For any continuous function f(x)f(x)f(x), ∫−∞∞f(x)δ(x−a)dx=f(a)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\delta(x-a) dx = f(a)∫−∞∞​f(x)δ(x−a)dx=f(a)

While the delta function is not a proper function, we can understand it as the limit of a sequence of functions. Let’s consider a rectangular pulse function:

δϵ(x)={1ϵif ∣x∣<ϵ20otherwise\delta_\epsilon(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\epsilon} & \text{if } |x| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}δϵ​(x)={ϵ1​0​if ∣x∣<2ϵ​otherwise​
(22)

The area under this function is:

∫−∞∞δϵ(x)dx=∫−ϵ/2ϵ/21ϵdx=1ϵ⋅ϵ=1\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta_\epsilon(x) dx = \int_{-\epsilon/2}^{\epsilon/2} \frac{1}{\epsilon} dx = \frac{1}{\epsilon} \cdot \epsilon = 1∫−∞∞​δϵ​(x)dx=∫−ϵ/2ϵ/2​ϵ1​dx=ϵ1​⋅ϵ=1
(23)

As ϵ→0\epsilon \to 0ϵ→0, δϵ(x)\delta_\epsilon(x)δϵ​(x) approaches the delta function, but the area remains 1.

Example 2: Transform of cos⁡(ω0t)\cos(\omega_0t)cos(ω0​t)¶

What the original figure plots. It shows periodic piecewise-linear wave and a low-order Fourier approximation.

What this is trying to convey. Piecewise-linear periodic-wave example preserved from Jonathan’s original notes and homework source.

Polished version.

f(t)=cos⁡(ω0t)\begin{aligned} f(t) &= \cos(\omega_0t) \end{aligned}f(t)​=cos(ω0​t)​
(24)
F(ω)=π[δ(ω−ω0)+δ(ω+ω0)]\begin{aligned} F(\omega) &= \pi [\delta(\omega-\omega_0) + \delta(\omega+\omega_0)] \end{aligned}F(ω)​=π[δ(ω−ω0​)+δ(ω+ω0​)]​
(25)

Explanation:

1) Express cosine in terms of complex exponentials: cos⁡(ω0t)=eiω0t+e−iω0t2\cos(\omega_0t) = \frac{e^{i\omega_0t} + e^{-i\omega_0t}}{2}cos(ω0​t)=2eiω0​t+e−iω0​t​

2) Take the Fourier transform of each term: F{eiω0t}=2πδ(ω−ω0)\mathcal{F}\{e^{i\omega_0t}\} = 2\pi\delta(\omega-\omega_0)F{eiω0​t}=2πδ(ω−ω0​) F{e−iω0t}=2πδ(ω+ω0)\mathcal{F}\{e^{-i\omega_0t}\} = 2\pi\delta(\omega+\omega_0)F{e−iω0​t}=2πδ(ω+ω0​)

3) Apply linearity and the factor of 1/2: F(ω)=12[2πδ(ω−ω0)+2πδ(ω+ω0)]F(\omega) = \frac{1}{2}[2\pi\delta(\omega-\omega_0) + 2\pi\delta(\omega+\omega_0)]F(ω)=21​[2πδ(ω−ω0​)+2πδ(ω+ω0​)]

This result shows that the Fourier transform of a cosine function consists of two delta functions: one at ω0\omega_0ω0​ and one at −ω0-\omega_0−ω0​, each with half the amplitude of the transform of the complex exponential. This reflects the fact that a cosine wave can be thought of as the sum of two rotating complex exponentials, one rotating positively and one negatively.

Fourier Transform Properties for Real Functions¶

If f(t)f(t)f(t) is real, then F(−ω)=F∗(ω)F(-\omega) = F^*(\omega)F(−ω)=F∗(ω)

Proof:

1. We assume f(t)f(t)f(t) is real-valued, i.e. f(t)=f∗(t)f(t) = f^*(t)f(t)=f∗(t).

2. Transform at −ω-\omega−ω:

F(−ω)=∫−∞∞f(t) e−i(−ω)t dt=∫−∞∞f(t) eiωt dt.F(-\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)\, e^{-i(-\omega)t}\, dt = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt.F(−ω)=∫−∞∞​f(t)e−i(−ω)tdt=∫−∞∞​f(t)eiωtdt.
(26)

3. Complex conjugate of F(ω)F(\omega)F(ω):

F∗(ω)=[∫−∞∞f(t) e−iωt dt]∗=∫−∞∞f∗(t) eiωt dt.F^*(\omega) = \left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)\, e^{-i\omega t}\, dt \right]^* = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f^*(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt.F∗(ω)=[∫−∞∞​f(t)e−iωtdt]∗=∫−∞∞​f∗(t)eiωtdt.
(27)

4. Since f∗(t)=f(t)f^*(t) = f(t)f∗(t)=f(t) (real function):

F∗(ω)=∫−∞∞f(t) eiωt dt.F^*(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt.F∗(ω)=∫−∞∞​f(t)eiωtdt.
(28)

Comparing with step 2, we find

F(−ω)=F∗(ω)\boxed{F(-\omega) = F^*(\omega)}F(−ω)=F∗(ω)​
(29)

Derivatives in Fourier Transforms¶

Given a function f(t)f(t)f(t), we want to find the Fourier transform of its derivative, i.e., F{dfdt}\mathcal{F}\left\{\frac{df}{dt}\right\}F{dtdf​}.

Proof:

Step 1: Definition of Fourier Transform:

F{g(t)}=∫−∞∞g(t)e−iωtdt\mathcal{F}\{g(t)\} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(t) e^{-i\omega t} dtF{g(t)}=∫−∞∞​g(t)e−iωtdt
(30)

Step 2: Apply definition to Derivative:

F{dfdt}=∫−∞∞dfdte−iωtdt\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}\left\{\frac{df}{dt}\right\} &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{df}{dt} e^{-i\omega t} dt \end{aligned}F{dtdf​}​=∫−∞∞​dtdf​e−iωtdt​
(31)

Step 3: Integration by parts: ∫u dv=uv−∫v du.\int u \,dv = uv - \int v \,du.∫udv=uv−∫vdu. In our case:

dv=dfdtdtu=e−iωtv=fdu=−iωe−iωtdt\begin{aligned} dv &= \frac{df}{dt}dt & u &= e^{-i\omega t} \\ v &= f & du &= -i\omega e^{-i\omega t}dt \end{aligned}dvv​=dtdf​dt=f​udu​=e−iωt=−iωe−iωtdt​
(32)

Derivatives in Fourier Transforms (continued)¶

Step 4: Apply Integration by Parts:

F{dfdt}=f(t)e−iωt∣t=−∞t=+∞−∫−∞∞f(t)(−iωe−iωt) dt=f(t)e−iωt∣−∞∞+iω∫−∞∞f(t)e−iωt dt=f(t)e−iωt∣−∞∞+iωF(ω).\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}\left\{\frac{df}{dt}\right\} &= \left. f(t)e^{-i\omega t}\right|_{t=-\infty}^{t=+\infty} - \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)\big(-i\omega e^{-i\omega t}\big)\,dt\\[6pt] &= \left. f(t)e^{-i\omega t}\right|_{-\infty}^{\infty} + i\omega \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)e^{-i\omega t}\,dt\\[6pt] &= \left. f(t)e^{-i\omega t}\right|_{-\infty}^{\infty} + i\omega F(\omega). \end{aligned}F{dtdf​}​=f(t)e−iωt∣∣​t=−∞t=+∞​−∫−∞∞​f(t)(−iωe−iωt)dt=f(t)e−iωt∣∣​−∞∞​+iω∫−∞∞​f(t)e−iωtdt=f(t)e−iωt∣∣​−∞∞​+iωF(ω).​
(33)

Step 5: Evaluate Limits

We assume sufficient decay or boundary behavior so that f(t)e−iωt∣−∞∞=0\left.f(t)e^{-i\omega t}\right|_{-\infty}^{\infty}=0f(t)e−iωt∣∣​−∞∞​=0.

Derivatives in Fourier Transforms (continued)¶

Step 6: Final Result

F{dfdt}=iωF(ω)=iωF{f(t)}.\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}\left\{\frac{df}{dt}\right\} &=i\omega F(\omega) =i\omega\mathcal{F}\{f(t)\}. \end{aligned}F{dtdf​}​=iωF(ω)=iωF{f(t)}.​
(34)

We have derived the important property:

This result shows that differentiation in the time domain corresponds to multiplication by iωi\omegaiω in the frequency domain. This property is fundamental in signal processing and differential equations.
